title: How to read a nutrition label

seo.title: How to read a Nutrition Facts label step by step
seo.meta_description: Learn how to interpret serving size, calories, saturated fat, sodium, fiber, added sugars, protein and % Daily Value on U.S. food labels.
seo.search_intent: Learn how to compare foods using the U.S. Nutrition Facts label and ingredient list.

excerpt: On a U.S. Nutrition Facts label, start with serving size and servings per container: every number below is tied to that amount. Then focus on the nutrients that matter for the product—such as protein, fiber, saturated fat, sodium and added sugars—and use % Daily Value as context rather than a score for the whole food.
content_html:
A Nutrition Facts panel can look like a wall of numbers, but you do not need to give every line equal attention. The useful approach is to answer three questions: How much am I actually eating? Which nutrients matter for this food? What is the product made from?

Start with serving size

On U.S. labels, calories and nutrient amounts are generally listed per labeled serving. If a package contains two servings and you eat the whole package, you are consuming roughly twice the listed calories, sodium, fat, carbohydrate and other nutrients.

Serving size is designed to reflect amounts people typically consume; it is not automatically a recommendation for how much you should eat.

It also helps to compare serving sizes before comparing two brands. If one granola lists a 30 g serving and another lists 55 g, the larger serving may look higher in calories simply because more food is being counted. Converting both to the same weight can separate a true composition difference from a portion-label difference.

Use calories in the context of the serving

If a food lists 180 calories per serving and the container holds three servings, the entire container contains about 540 calories. That arithmetic is often more useful than deciding whether 180 is “high” or “low” in isolation.

Calorie density also changes what a normal serving looks like. Nuts, oils, cheese, fruit, soup, and yogurt should not be judged as if 100 calories represented the same amount of food. The number is most useful when tied to the quantity you are actually planning to eat.

The lines that usually deserve attention

Label itemWhat it tells you
Total FatAll fat in the serving
Saturated FatThe saturated portion of total fat
SodiumSodium in milligrams
Total CarbohydrateTotal carbohydrate including fiber and sugars
Dietary FiberFiber in the serving
Total SugarsNaturally occurring + added sugars
Includes Added SugarsSugars added during processing
ProteinTotal protein in the serving

Which lines matter most depends on the product. For bread you may care about fiber and sodium; for yogurt, protein and added sugar; for a frozen entrée, sodium may be especially useful. Focusing on two or three relevant numbers is usually more informative than treating every row as equally important.

Total Sugars and Added Sugars answer different questions

Plain milk or yogurt contains lactose, so it can show Total Sugars even when no sugar was added. The separate Added Sugars line helps distinguish that from sugar, syrups or other caloric sweeteners added during manufacturing.

For example, a plain yogurt might contain 6 g Total Sugars and 0 g Added Sugars, while a flavored version could contain 17 g Total Sugars including 11 g Added Sugars.

This distinction is especially useful for dairy and fruit-based foods, where some sugar comes with the basic ingredient. Total Sugars still tells you how much sugar is present overall; Added Sugars helps explain how much was introduced during manufacturing.

What % Daily Value actually means

% Daily Value (%DV) shows how much a nutrient in one serving contributes to the FDA's reference Daily Value. As a general label-reading shortcut, FDA describes 5% DV or less as low and 20% DV or more as high for a nutrient.

That does not make 20% automatically “good” or “bad.” A high %DV for fiber may be useful; a high %DV for sodium may be something you want to compare carefully.

Daily Values are reference numbers, not personal prescriptions. Your own energy and nutrient needs can differ, but %DV is still handy for comparing similar foods without having to memorize milligram targets for every nutrient.

The ingredient list answers a different question

Ingredients are listed separately in descending order by weight. The first few usually make up most of the product. This can help distinguish, for example, a whole-grain bread whose first ingredient is whole-wheat flour from one where refined flour dominates.

It also shows added sweeteners, oils, protein isolates, flavors and other ingredients that are not obvious from the front of the package.

A long ingredient list is not automatically worse than a short one. What matters is what the main ingredients are and whether they match the product you think you are buying. The list can clarify how much whole grain, what type of oil, or which sweeteners are actually present.

Do not judge every food by the same nutrient

A cheese may be high in sodium and saturated fat while also providing protein and calcium. Nuts are high in calories and fat but often rich in unsaturated fat, fiber and minerals. A sweetened cereal may be low in total fat yet high in added sugar.

The label works best when you ask a specific question rather than searching for one number that certifies the entire product.

A 30-second routine

  1. Check serving size and servings per container.
  2. Adjust the numbers to the amount you will actually eat.
  3. Focus on two or three nutrients relevant to that food.
  4. Use %DV for context.
  5. Read the first few ingredients.
  6. Compare products that serve a similar role.

That turns the Nutrition Facts panel from a list to memorize into a practical comparison tool.

If two similar products remain very close after that check, tiny nutrient differences may not deserve much weight. Price, taste, convenience, and the amount you are likely to eat can be more useful decision factors than chasing a one-gram difference that will barely change the meal.

faq.question: What should I look at first on a Nutrition Facts label?
faq.answer: Serving size and servings per container, because every calorie and nutrient number is tied to that amount.

faq.question: What is the difference between Total Sugars and Added Sugars?
faq.answer: Total Sugars includes naturally occurring sugars plus added sugars. Added Sugars reports only sugars added during processing.

faq.question: Is 20% Daily Value high?
faq.answer: FDA uses 20% DV or more as a general high benchmark and 5% DV or less as low, but whether high is desirable depends on the nutrient.
